{{Short description|Theorem in complex analysis}}
In [[complex analysis]], a branch of mathematics, the '''Hadamard three-line theorem''' is a result about the behaviour of [[holomorphic function]]s defined in regions bounded by parallel lines in the [[complex plane]].  The theorem is named after the French mathematician [[Jacques Hadamard]].

== Statement ==

{{math theorem|name=Hadamard three-line theorem|note=|style=|math_statement= 
Let <math>f(z)</math> be a [[bounded function]] of <math>z = x + i y</math> defined on the strip

:<math>\{ x + iy : a \leq x \leq b \},</math>

holomorphic in the interior of the strip and continuous on the whole strip. If

:<math>M(x) = \sup_y |f(x+iy)|</math>

then <math>\log M(x)</math> is a [[convex function]] on <math>[a, b].</math>

In other words, if <math>x = t a + (1-t) b</math> with <math>0 \leq t \leq 1,</math> then

:<math>M(x) \leq M(a)^t M(b)^{1-t}.</math>
}}

{{collapse top|title=Proof|left=true}}
Define <math> F(z)</math> by

:<math> F(z)=f(z) M(a)^{{z-b\over b-a}}M(b)^{{z-a\over a-b}}</math>

where <math>|F(z)| \leq 1</math> on the edges of the strip. The result follows once it is shown that the inequality also holds in the interior of the strip. 
After an [[affine transformation]] in the coordinate <math>z,</math> it can be assumed that <math>a = 0</math> and <math>b = 1.</math>
The function

:<math> F_n(z) = F(z) e^{z^2/n}e^{-1/n} </math>

tends to <math>0</math> as <math>|z|</math> tends to infinity and satisfies <math>|F_n| \leq 1</math> on the boundary of the strip. The [[maximum modulus principle]] can therefore be applied to <math>F_n</math> in the strip. So <math>|F_n(z)| \leq 1.</math> Because <math>F_n(z)</math> tends to <math>F(z)</math> as <math>n</math> tends to infinity, it follows that <math>|F(z)| \leq 1.</math> ∎
{{collapse bottom}} 

== Applications ==
The three-line theorem can be used to prove the [[Hadamard three-circle theorem]] for a bounded continuous function <math>g(z)</math> on an
[[Annulus (mathematics)|annulus]] <math>\{ z: r \leq |z| \leq R \},</math> holomorphic in the interior. Indeed applying the theorem to

:<math>f(z) = g(e^{z}),</math>

shows that, if

:<math>m(s) = \sup_{|z| = e^s} |g(z)|,</math>

then <math>\log\, m(s)</math> is a convex function of <math>s.</math>

The three-line theorem also holds for functions with values in a [[Banach space]] and plays an important role in [[Interpolation space#Complex interpolation|complex interpolation theory]]. It can be used to prove [[Hölder's inequality]] for measurable functions

:<math>\int |gh| \leq \left(\int |g|^p\right)^{1\over p} \cdot \left(\int |h|^q\right)^{1\over q},</math>

where <math>{1\over p} + {1\over q} = 1,</math> by considering the function

:<math>f(z) = \int |g|^{pz} |h|^{q(1-z)}.</math>
